findings.title: Recovery codes stored in user storage are never consumed after successful use
findings.body: When a user's recovery codes live in a user-storage provider (the capability this PR adds), a successfully used code is never invalidated. For locally stored codes, single-use semantics are enforced inside RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid(), which removes the used code from the stored credential. In the federated path, RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.isRecoveryAuthnCodeInputValid() calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().isValid(...), which delegates to the storage provider's CredentialInputValidator.isValid(), and the framework performs no consumption step afterwards. The PR's own reference implementation (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid) only compares the presented code against the stored list and never removes it. Consequences: every recovery code remains valid indefinitely, breaking the one-time-use guarantee of the feature; RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.allCodesUsed() never becomes true, so the user is never forced to regenerate codes and the login form always asks for code #1; and even if a storage did consume codes itself, the cleanup call authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()) operates on Keycloak's local credential store and cannot remove a credential living in user storage. The feature needs a consumption/update mechanism for federated credentials (e.g., writing the reduced code list back through CredentialInputUpdater.updateCredential after a successful validation) or the limitation must be explicitly handled.

findings.title: Plaintext recovery codes are pushed to user storage while local storage keeps only hashes
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated recovery codes (JsonSerialization.writeValueAsString(generatedCodes)) and sends them to the user storage via a UserCredentialModel. When the same credential is stored locally, RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues() hashes every code via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode() so only hashes are persisted (verification is done with verifyRecoveryCodeInput against the hash). Unlike OTP secrets — which an external store genuinely needs in clear text to compute TOTP — recovery-code verification can be performed by hashing the presented code, so there is no technical need to hand the raw codes to the user storage. As implemented, any external user storage that opts into recovery codes ends up holding every user's recovery codes in clear text (and the codes transit in clear through CredentialInput.getChallengeResponse()), so a read-breach of that store, its backups, or its logs exposes all of a user's recovery codes. Consider sending hashed codes to the storage and documenting that storages should hash the presented code in isValid(), matching the local storage security posture.

findings.title: New recovery-keys test never verifies single-use semantics
findings.body: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin performs only one successful login with one recovery code. It never attempts to reuse the same code, never checks that the remaining-code count decreases, and never exercises the all-codes-used path (credential removal and re-adding the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action). Because of this, the test passes even though recovery codes stored in user storage are currently reusable after a successful login — the core security property of the feature is unverified. The test should at minimum assert that a second login attempt with the same code fails and that a subsequent login requests a different code number.
